sentences.text: The body of this ancient fish was protected by bony plates covering the head and the front part of the trunk.
Its head featured a distinctive keyhole-shaped opening on top for the eyes and nostrils, while the mouth was located on the lower front side.
In mature adults, the two halves of the jaw operated as separate, functionally independent units.
Behind the armored head, the trunk was likely slender and covered in soft skin rather than scales or patterns.
Modern classification recognizes only a single, high, and rounded dorsal fin positioned toward the rear of the animal.
Unlike typical fish, the gill region was positioned higher up, crowded toward the front, and was relatively short and broad.
Excavations at the Catskill Formation site revealed more than two hundred individuals packed tightly together.
The genus was first formally described by Eichwald in the year 1840.
The species B. canadensis was initially named by J.F. Whiteaves in 1880.
Another species, B. coloradensis, was described by Eastman in 1904 from remains found in present-day Colorado.
Fossils of B. africana have been recovered exclusively from the Witpoort Formation near Makhanda in South Africa.
The largest known species, B. rex, was originally described by Downs et al. in 2016 from the Nordstrand Point Formation of Ellesmere Island, Canada.
Most species were small, bottom-dwelling freshwater detritivores averaging about 30 cm in length.
They fed by swallowing mouthfuls of mud and soft sediments to digest detritus, microorganisms, algae, and organic matter.
The ventral positioning of the mouth suggests that this animal was a dedicated bottom-feeder.
Researchers suggest the animal used its spike-like pectoral fins to lift its armored body off the bottom.
Its digestive system possessed a specialized complex spiral valve, similar to that found in some sharks.
Robert Denison published a paper exploring the soft anatomy and organs of this creature.
Downs et al. (2016) suggest that the thick armor of B. rex served to protect against predators and acted as ballast to prevent the large bottom-dweller from floating.
Fossils are found in strata dating from 387 to 360 million years ago.
The time range for the genus extends from the Emsian to the Famennian stages, between 410.62 and 358.86 million years ago.
It inhabited near-shore marine and freshwater environments across all paleocontinents.
Fossils have been found in Asia, Europe, Australia, Africa, North America, and South America.
It is unclear exactly when gnathostomes emerged, though the fossil record suggests the Early Palaeozoic era.
It is debated whether Bothriolepis had a notochord, as the trunk outline suggests one but no direct evidence exists due to soft tissue decay.
It is debated whether the ventral sacs of Bothriolepis functioned as lungs that allowed the animal to travel on land.
It is debated whether B. coloradensis is similar to or identical to B. nitida due to the fragmented nature of the available material.
There is significant debate regarding whether B. nitida and B. virginiensis can be distinguished from one another.
